problem: DRL-based social navigation planners have fixed, converged policies that cannot adapt to real-time user commands or feedback (e.g. changed social distance or goal) or to zero-shot environments. LLM-based planners usually output only macro-actions or semantic goals, and are unreliable on continuous numeric control in crowds.
motivation: Interactive social robots, for example in cooperative carrying, must follow volatile human language requests and personal preferences while staying socially compliant. DRL gives a robust baseline but is rigid. LLMs give flexible semantic reasoning but hallucinate and handle numbers poorly, so combining them should give both adaptability and robustness.
key_idea: Run an LLM-based low-level navigation model (LNM) and a DRL policy (RLNM, NaviSTAR-based) in parallel from high-level LLM-parsed user guidance, then fuse their velocity actions with weights scored by a Graph-of-Thoughts LLM feedback model (LFM).
insight: The ablations show that neither component suffices alone. RLNM-only (SA-RLNM) keeps its old strategy after user feedback, while LNM-only (SA-LNM) oscillates side to side in crowds (SR 62 vs 86 for full SALM). Fixed 0.5/0.5 fusion (SA-LFM) gives SR 63, well below the adaptive GoT-scored fusion at 86, so the gain comes from context-dependent weighting rather than from simply ensembling the two planners.
method: High-level user-parsing LLM: converts language commands and feedback into global guidance (task type P2P or human-following, target, privacy distance, pedestrian-first or robot-first norm) and replans it on new feedback.

LNM (large language navigation model): an image-to-text encoder turns robot and pedestrian states into text. A structured prompt (task description, global guidance, data annotation, demonstration/history from a memory buffer, additional info) makes GPT-4o output low-level velocity [vx, vy].

RLNM: a NaviSTAR-based DRL planner using a spatio-temporal transformer with cross-attention fusion. It is conditioned on the LLM guidance and outputs macro- and local actions under a Dec-POSMDP formulation.

LFM (large language feedback model): a 4-layer Graph-of-Thoughts prompt with generation, aggregation, refining and scoring operations. It verifies a_RL, a_LM and the pair using checklists, then outputs the relative weights (s1, s2).
Execution decoder: a_R = Decoder(s1*a_RL + s2*a_LM) gives the final action.
Memory mechanism: demonstrations are replaced by executed history, which supplies long-term feedback to LNM and LFM.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, for LLM/LNM/LFM) + NaviSTAR-style spatio-temporal transformer DRL policy (RLNM)
setting.training_data: RLNM trained with DRL in the gym social-navigation simulator (NaviSTAR setup); the LLM parts are training-free prompting
setting.observation: robot local observation of positions, velocities and radii of humans and robot, converted to text for the LLM and to an ST-graph for the DRL policy
setting.action_space: continuous 2D velocity [vx, vy] (plus macro-actions such as waypoints or targets)
setting.simulator: gym-based social navigation simulator (NaviSTAR / NaviDiff) with ORCA-simulated pedestrians, extended with language commands and feedback
setting.privileged: none stated (robot-estimable observable states; pedestrian goals and preferences are unobserved)

numbers_note: The only benchmark is the authors' custom simulator, so the numbers are not comparable to standard benchmarks. No SD or error bars are reported, and no NE or SPL metrics.
results: SALM reaches an average SR of 86 and SS of 82, beating NaviSTAR (74 / 68), SRNN (75 / 54), CADRL (58 / 57) and ORCA (31 / 30) with LLM goal parsing. It also beats all three ablations (SA-RLNM 75 / 74, SA-LNM 62 / 53, SA-LFM 63 / 59).
limitations: Evaluated only in a custom simulator with 50 test cases per task and simulated random user feedback. There is no real-robot experiment and no statistical analysis.
Depends on GPT-4o with multi-step GoT prompting, which adds latency and cost and could hurt real-time control. Latency is not reported.
Text-encoded numeric states make LNM alone unstable (oscillation), and the paper gives few implementation details (prompts, LFM weight ranges, RL training setup).
